Description: Detected a Generic API Key, potentially exposing access to various services and sensitive operations.
Author: SanOft
Message:
feat(api): authentication — argon2, pinned JWT, refresh rotation and reuse detection

Registration and login (FR-1, FR-2)
- Argon2id at OWASP's m=19456, t=2, p=1. The test reads those back out of the
  PHC string rather than from the constant the code passes, because asserting
  a value against itself proves nothing.
- `verifySecret` returns false on a malformed digest instead of throwing. That
  case is real: the SYSTEM account's passwordHash is a sentinel (§9.4), and a
  login attempt against it must be an ordinary failure rather than a 500 that
  tells the caller they found something unusual.
- Registration creates the user and their UZS account in one transaction, and
  catches the uniqueness violation rather than pre-checking it — a SELECT then
  INSERT has a window where two concurrent registrations both see the number
  as free. Every rejection returns the identical generic body (FR-1.5).
- Login spends the same time whether or not the number exists, by verifying
  against a pre-computed throwaway digest. Returning early is the natural way
  to write this and it is exactly what S-5 tests for: argon2 at m=19456 takes
  tens of milliseconds, so the fast path would be audible. The digest is
  computed once at startup, not per request, which would be a free DoS lever.

Tokens (FR-2.4 to FR-2.7)
- `jose` rather than `jsonwebtoken`: zero dependencies against ten, six of them
  lodash micro-packages. For the library guarding authentication that decides
  it. It also refuses to verify without an explicit algorithm list.
- HS256 is pinned in both directions, and issuer and audience are checked, so a
  token minted for another service cannot be replayed here. Tests forge
  `alg: none` and `alg: HS512` and watch both fail.
- JWT_SECRET is rejected below 32 characters at boot. A short secret is not
  "weaker but working" — it is the only thing between a forged token and an
  authenticated request, and a deploy using `changeme` would look identical to
  a correct one.
- Refresh tokens are opaque 256-bit values stored as SHA-256 digests (§9.2), not
  JWTs: revocation needs the database anyway, so signing would add risk and
  nothing else (§21 Q-5). SHA-256 rather than Argon2 because the input is our
  own randomness — there is nothing to brute-force and no reason to pay Argon2
  on the hot refresh path.
- Rotation and reuse detection: a token that has already been exchanged coming
  back means either the client replayed it or someone else holds a copy. We
  cannot tell which, so the whole family is revoked and every device signs in
  again. S-4 asserts that the *legitimate* device is signed out too, not only
  the replayed token.

Response validation (T-3.8)
- `respond()` serialises every success through a Zod schema. The shared
  `auth.ts` comment claims a Prisma record parsed through `publicUserSchema`
  has its hash stripped; this is the thing that does the parsing, so the
  guarantee is structural rather than a promise. Forgetting a field now shows
  up as a missing field rather than an invisible leak.

Cookies (FR-2.4)
- httpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure outside development, 30 days, scoped to
  /api/auth. Read with a ten-line parser rather than cookie-parser: the only
  cookie this service reads holds a base64url value of our own making, so none
  of the escaping cases that justify the dependency can arise. The comment says
  to use the library if that ever stops being true.

Also
- Verified before adopting: argon2 loads with Yarn's build scripts disabled,
  because node-gyp-build resolves a prebuilt binary at require time.
- Tests build the app through one helper that calls `createApp` exactly as
  index.ts does. The day 2 review found three defects that survived because
  every test assembled its own middleware stack.

Refs runbook T-3.1 to T-3.8; FR-1, FR-2, NFR-1.1, NFR-1.2, NFR-1.4, NFR-1.5,
NFR-1.6; S-4, S-5.
